searchNote: About 25 web searches ran and then the per-turn search budget was exhausted. WebFetch could not reach Wikipedia (DNS failure). Claims not reached by a search were judged from solid prior knowledge and the library's own entries (node scripts/library-hub.mjs); they are listed under remainingDoubts. Counts below are approximate tallies of the individual checkable claims.

softened.was: In the early nineteenth century the verse tale reached a wide public: Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancient Mariner (1798) set the literary ballad, Scott's The Lady of the Lake (1810) and Byron's The Giaour (1813) and The Corsair (1814) found large audiences.
softened.now: Around 1800 the verse tale reached a wide public: Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancient Mariner (1798) became a landmark of the literary ballad, and Scott's The Lady of the Lake (1810) and Byron's The Giaour (1813) and The Corsair (1814) found large audiences.
softened.why: 1798 is not the early nineteenth century, and 'set the literary ballad' implied the Mariner founded the literary ballad, which Percy-inspired German and English writers had already begun.

softened.was: Pope's The Rape of the Lock (1712)
softened.now: Pope's The Rape of the Lock (first version 1712)
softened.why: Search confirmed the 1712 text is the two-canto first version; the five-canto poem is 1714 and the form was revised again in 1717.

softened.was: verse novels for young readers are shelved with children's and teen fiction rather than poetry.
softened.now: verse novels for young readers are usually sold as children's and teen fiction rather than as poetry, though some libraries shelve them with poetry.
softened.why: Shelving varies by shop and library (some classify verse novels with poetry); the flat claim was too strong for a 'varies' record.

softened.was: The market for book-length narrative poems for adults is small and mostly served by poetry and university presses
softened.now: The market for book-length narrative poems for adults is small and sits mainly on the poetry lists of publishers large and small
softened.why: Landmark examples in the same file (Seth, Walcott, Carson, Oswald) came from large trade houses, so 'mostly poetry and university presses' could not be defended.

softened.was: many readers meet them as performances or audio
softened.now: some readers meet them as performances or audio

remainingDoubts: Aurora Leigh is dated 1856 (published November 1856; the title page reads 1857). Agrees with the library and is the usual convention.
Gilgamesh 'over three thousand years' and Homer 'about the eighth century BCE' are the safe general dates; scholars range wider for Homer.

corrected.was: in 1990 in San Francisco with a handful of city teams
corrected.now: in 1990 in San Francisco with teams from only a few cities
corrected.why: 1990, San Francisco and Fort Mason confirmed; accounts give about three teams (Chicago, San Francisco and New York), with disagreement over whether New York sent a team or invited poets. 'A handful' overstated it.

corrected.was: a practice with roots in Black church, jazz and hip-hop traditions.
corrected.now: a practice with deep roots in African American music and the Black church, and one that jazz and hip-hop carried on.
corrected.why: Call and response is older than jazz and hip-hop; the earlier wording implied those genres were roots rather than inheritors.

softened.was: when the poet Marc Kelly Smith's reading series, held at the Green Mill Jazz Club, took on a contest format scored by judges from the audience
softened.now: when the poet Marc Kelly Smith's reading series, which became based at the Green Mill Jazz Club, took on a contest format scored by judges from the audience
softened.why: Sources put his Chicago series at the Get Me High Lounge from late 1984 and the Green Mill's Uptown Poetry Slam from 25 July 1986; the old wording implied the contest format began at the Green Mill. The new wording avoids the sequence.

softened.was: The Last Poets (formed in Harlem in 1968)
softened.now: The Last Poets (first performing in Harlem in 1968)
softened.why: A first public performance in Harlem on 19 May 1968 is well supported, but sources disagree on founders and the better-known lineup came from a 1969 workshop. The existing watch line about changing membership still applies.

remainingDoubts: Slam scoring and time rules (about three minutes, five judges, zero to ten, high and low dropped, props and music barred) match common Poetry Slam Inc style practice and are flagged as varying by event, which the text already says.
Nuyorican Poets Cafe: 1973 start in Algarin's apartment confirmed, but sources differ on founders (Algarin alone, or with Pinero and others) and on exact date; the text names only Algarin and no day.

corrected.why: Search confirmed Lenore was written in 1773 and first published in 1774 in the Gottinger Musenalmanach; the library convention is first-publication year.

corrected.was: The earliest surviving English ballad texts are from the late Middle Ages: Robin Hood and the Monk survives in a manuscript of about 1450 and A Gest of Robyn Hode was printed around 1500;
corrected.now: Some English ballad texts survive from the Middle Ages: Robin Hood and the Monk is in a manuscript of about 1450, and A Gest of Robyn Hode survives in editions printed in the decades around 1500;
corrected.why: Judas (Child 23) is generally dated to the thirteenth century, so these are not the earliest surviving texts; and the Gest's early editions are dated from the 1490s (Pynson fragments) to about 1510 (de Worde, Antwerp), so 'around 1500' was too precise.

corrected.was: holds a great many from the later seventeenth century.
corrected.now: holds a great many, mostly from the seventeenth century.
corrected.why: The collection holds over 1,800 ballads, mostly of the seventeenth century; volume 1 rests on John Selden's earlier collection, so 'later seventeenth century' was too narrow.

softened.was: known in English from the late Middle Ages
softened.now: known in English from the Middle Ages
softened.why: Judas is a thirteenth-century text; the broader phrase agrees with the corrected point above.

softened.was: traditional ballads run from a few stanzas to several dozen,
softened.now: traditional ballads usually run from a few stanzas to several dozen,
softened.why: General estimate; 'usually' keeps it true given longer outliers.

remainingDoubts: Ballad origins are disputed (communal composition versus individual and minstrel composers); the history record is correctly set to contested and says so in watch.
